articleTitle: Pulsed electro-acoustic method for the measurement of volume charges in E-beam irradiated PMMA
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: The measurement of volume charges within insulators has been attempted by various methods, including thermal, optical, mechanical, and electrical stimulation of the sample. A new method incorporating pulse electrical stimulation and pulsed acoustic detection is reported here. This technique is an extension of a previously reported [1] high frequency AC steady state electro-acoustic measurements in which electric fields at an electrode surface are determined by measuring the AC high frequency vibration of the electrode in response to a DC plus high frequency AC excitation. The use of pulse operation allows the measurements of time domain delay information which yields the spatial distribution of the volume charge.

articleTitle: Space charge injection in polymers: New experimental results
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: For a long time treeing has been known as a major mechanism responsible for ageing of technical insulations, which can subsequently lead to their catastrophic breakdown. According to its importance, treeing is the subject of a vast number of publications /1/. Tree initiation and the conditions for tree growth, however, have been studied to a much lesser extent. In a recent paper /2/ this problem is treated phenomenologically in analogy to classical fracture mechanics /3/. An electro-mechanical fracture criterion has been introduced, stating that a tree can only grow if the release of electrostatic energy is larger than the mechanical deformation energy needed to form microchannels, i.e. trees.

articleTitle: Partial discharge deterioration of epoxy resin for electronic parts
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: Recently many electronic parts are widely used for the power electric field, such as power transistor module, diode and solid state relay. These are encapsulated with solid insulating materials such as epoxy resin or silicon rubber. In these category of parts, majority of electrical failures has been caused by inadequate material selection or workmanship error for encapsulation systems. It is suspected that the cause of the electrical failures is due to partial discharge (PD) in voids of insulating materials or in cracks in the vicinity of conductors. Accordingly, the test on PD has been performed for these products. Although PD quantity (e.g. PD current, Qmax), decreases gradually during voltage application with ordinary electrical PD measurements, while solid insulating materials degrade along with time and finally result in electrical breakdown [1,2].

articleTitle: Ion production rates in SF6 and the relevance thereof to gas-insulated switchgear
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: Breakdown of SF<inf>6</inf> is of commercial interest as a result of the large amounts of SF<inf>6</inf>-insulated switchgear installed world wide and is of technical interest as a result of the excellent dielectric strength of the gas caused by its high electronegativity. Previous studies in the area of positive surge breakdown area have centered on the concept of “critical volume”. The basic idea has been that probability of breakdown depends on the volume stressed above the minimum breakdown voltage and the electron production rate [1-2]. These concepts are semi-empirically based and have been derived under relatively homogeneous field conditions. As such, one has no reason to think that the concepts have any fundamental or universal validity.

articleTitle: Partial discharge characteristics in phase domain for various cylindrical voids
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: As the shape and the size of a void in a insulation system affect considerably the progress of the deterioration of the insulation performance if partial discharges (PD's) occur in the void, it is important to estimate both of the two parameters. Conventional PD characteristics are however ineffective to estimate the shape of a void. Therefore the relationship between the shape of a cylindrical void and the statistical characteristics of PD's occurring in the void is investigated in terms of φ-q distribution profile as well as conventional PD characteristics such as the maximum apparent discharge magnitude (qmax). The φ-q distribution profile describes the average pulse height as a function of the phase angle of an applied AC voltage and was found to be sensitive to the structure of a void in which PD's occurred[1].

articleTitle: A model for space charge injection in dielectrics
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: Space charges are known to play a very important role in dielectric ageing. The difference between impulse and dc electric strength, the influence of prestressing and impulse rise time on breakdown voltages and the polarity dependence of the breakdown voltage in the needle plate geometry all have been explained by space charge build up (1). In addition, the action of highly energetic charge carriers are often held responsible for the initiation of electrical trees (2). In a recent publication (3) it has been shown that growth of an electrical tree is possible if the mechanical stress at the tip of a discharge channel exceeds the local yield stress of the dielectric. Both quantities are strongly influenced by space charge injection because the mechanical stress is directly dependent on the space charge distribution ρ(x) through the force field f(x) = ρ(x) · F(x), and the local yield stress may be reduced by the injection of charge through local heating or plasma chemical damage. The latter effects will be particularly important under ac conditions.

articleTitle: Electrical performance of polymer insulating materials: Effect of material and filler type
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: The ac surface ageing of high temperature vulcanized (HTV) silicone rubber, ethylene propylene rubber (EPR) and cycloaliphatic epoxy is investigated in a salt-fog chamber. The silicone rubber (SR) and epoxy samples are filled with alumina trihydrate (ΑΤΗ). The EPR samples are filled with either ΑΤΗ or silica. The filler concentration is varied over a wide range. Testing is conducted at three electrical stresses centered around the average value used in practice and a microprocessor based system is used for data acquisition.

articleTitle: Effects of hydrostatic pressure on the prebreakdown phenomena in dielectric liquids
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: It is commonly accepted that a gaseous phase is involved during the prebreakdown phase of dielectric liquid breakdown. This is indicated by the generation of gas bubbles following streamer propagation, whatever the polarity. It has been known for a long time that increasing the pressure vastly improves the breakdown voltage whether DC or AC. KAO and McMATH [1] have shown that in. a quasi-uniform field, the effects of the pressure on the breakdown voltage became negligible for sufficiently short rise times of the voltage ramp. In point-plane geometry, it has been reported that an increase in pressure reduced the prebreakdown light emission [2]. The rise time and the peak value of prebreakdown current in a parallel plate arrangement with a small protrusion on one electrode decreased with increase in pressure [3]. Time lags to prebreakdown disturbances increased with hydrostatic pressure, the pressure dependence decreasing at very high voltages [4]. The purpose of this paper is to study in the point-plane geometry with rectangular voltage pulses, the influence of the pressure both on the initiation and the propagation phases, by recording the streamer velocity, the transient currents and light emission.

articleTitle: A new method for the location of partial discharge sites using modulated X-rays
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: It has been known for at least 20 years that X-rays passing through a partial discharge may modify both discharge magnitude and repetition rate. The effect is subtle, however, and may be completely masked by discharge signals from other sites. A new method has been proposed and experimentally verified wherein discharge sites are found by scanning an insulation system with a modulated X-ray beam, and subsequently recovering a signal at the modulation frequency from the output of a conventional PD detector, using correlation and/or spectral analysis techniques. As a test object is scanned by the X-ray beam, knowledge of PD sites is obtained when a signal at the modulating frequency is recovered. The technique is applicable to a wide range of practical insulation systems and offers high spatial resolution and noise immunity.

articleTitle: Additives for the inhibition of water trees and phenomenological aspects of water treeing
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: Water-trees result when polyethylene (PE) or cross-linked polyethylene (XLPE) is electrically stressed in a moist environment /l/. The experimental results do not present a unified picture and the literature abounds with at times rather controversial results regarding the influence of the electric field strength, the frequency, the type of electrolyte, the temperature and the insulating material. Apparently, the initiation and growth of water-trees are rather complex processes which are influenced, in addition, by boundary conditions such as the type of sample used, the method of sample preparation and the selection and combination of stressing conditions. For this reason, we concerned ourselves in particular with defect sites at which the trees originate, with structural aspects of these trees, and with conditions relevant for initiation. Based on these phenomenological investigations a model of water tree formation was developed and used in the search for water tree inhibiting additives.

articleTitle: Time-induced partial discharge breakdown in laminate structures
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: Insulating materials play a key role in the design and reliable performance of high voltage power equipment. It is well known that most of the failure in electrical apparatus occurs due to electrical breakdown of the insulating medium. Therefore, understanding the mechanism of the failure of the electrical insulation, especially under long-term exposure to high electric fields, and developing techniques to improve reliability of these materials is important for the design of efficient high voltage systems.

articleTitle: An investigation into water trees: Existence of channels and the influence of crosslinking
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: There are several published theories that attempt to explain the basic mechanisms of water treeing [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. They can be divided into the mechanistic theories and chemical damage theories. The mechanistic theories attempt to explain water treeing in terms of the electromechanical forces caused by dielectrophoresis, Maxwell stresses, Coulombic interactions, and changes in the chemical potential in regions of high electrical stress causing a high concentration of water and a subsequent pressure rise. It is claimed by the mechanistic theories that forces can exceed the tensile strength of the polymer and cause rupturing of the molecular chains. In the chemical damage theories water treeing is believed to be due to polymer water physichochemical interactions involving changes in the material properties of the insulation.

articleTitle: Dielectric properties of plasma-deposited thin films: A comparison of different materials
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: Thin films deposited in low pressure glow discharges are finding application in various areas: silicon nitride (P-SiN), oxide (P-SiO<inf>2</inf>) and oxynitride (P-SiON), all good insulators, are used in integrated circuit technology as passivation layers and dielectrics, whereas organic plasma polymers show promise as capacitor dielectrics. These latter materials, however, have a strong tendency to age, which has so far always led to unacceptably high dielectric losses<sup>[1]</sup>.

articleTitle: In situ infrared spectroscopy of electric field induced microstructural changes in polyethylene
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: Application of an electric field on a polymer leads to microstructural and morphology changes, interpreted as electrical aging, which eventually lead to dielectric breakdown. Infrared spectroscopy is a diagnostic technique which gives information on the microstructure of the materials. However, spectra taken days after the removal of a high electric field on the materials show little influence [1] probably because of the relaxation of the molecular chains. Therefore, in situ infrared spectroscopy of the materials under high electric field is a more appropriate method of studying field induced structural changes which sould lead to a better understanding of electrical aging.

articleTitle: Effects of space charge on electrical conduction in polyethylene
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: Many factors are known to affect the electrical conduction and breakdown of polymeric insulating materials. Among them the space charge effect is one of the most serious problems. For example, Bradwell et al. [1] and Ieda and Nawata [2] reported that the build-up of space charge remarkably affected the electrical strength and the DC treeing breakdown characteristics of polyethylene (PE). Not many papers, however, have been published on the quantitative estimation of space charge and its relation to conduction and breakdown phenomena. In this paper, the space charge in PE has been probed by using modified thermal pulse technique, which utilizes displacement current induced by nonuniform thermal expansion of a specimen under pulse-like heating (TPC: thermal pulse current). The nature of space charge and the effect of space charge on electrical conduction have been discussed quantitatively.

articleTitle: The application of high repetition rate voltage pulses to electrical and thermal aging
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: A critical factor in the research and development of a new insulation system is the accurate assessment of its reliability and expected lifetime during service. The methods to determine reliability generally attempt to accelerate the degradation processes that normally occur in electrical insulation over an extended operating time period. To date, most accelerated aging studies have featured test voltage frequencies and/or temperatures that far exceed typical operating levels. However, these efforts have not been completely successful due to the lack of knowledge concerning the relationships between the temperature, frequency of applied voltage, and the physical mechanisms responsible for dielectric deterioration and breakdown.

articleTitle: Effect of wind and de-icing on the minimum flashover voltage of H.V. insulators
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: A string of classic glass insulators and fog-type porcelain insulators were subjected to the simultaneous effects of ac high-voltage, hard rain and wind. The experiments were performed in a cold room with a H.V. transformer of 125 kVA, 120 kV. A high voltage, 15 kV per unit insulator, was applied to a vertical string of insulators during the icing period. When the thickness of ice on the monitoring conductor was 2 cm, the tap water spray was stopped and the wind was allowed to blow. The applied voltage was then increased at a rate of 6.3 kV/s. For the wind velocity having the maximum of 5.5 m/s, it is found that the minimum flashover voltage, V<inf>MF</inf>, of the porcelain insulators is about 142% more than that of the insulators without wind. These results show that the increase of V<inf>MF</inf> with the wind is due to the freezing of the water film on the surface of accreted ice. Iced insulators were tested also during de-icing period. After accretion, the spray was stopped and the ambient temperature was raised at different rates. Mien the ice temperature was about −1.5°C, the high voltage was increased. It is found that V<inf>MF</inf> during the de-icing period is approximately the same as that of the insulator during the icing period.

articleTitle: The influence of TiO2 and BaTiO3 additives on the space charge distribution in LDPE
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: The effect of TiO<inf>2</inf> and BaTiO<inf>3</inf> on space charge formation under HVDC in thick LDPE specimens has been investigated using a field probe technique. In plain LDPE the distribution is of the homocharge type, in TiO<inf>2</inf>-doped LDPE the distribution shows a prevailing negative charge and in BaTiO<inf>3</inf>-doped LDPE the distribution is complex and shows the formation of hetero- and homocharges. In all cases it was found that the space charge distribution is dependent on the duration of the applied voltage. The presence of additives also influences the evolution of space charges with time. X-ray diffraction patterns for both plain and doped LDPE have been obtained.

articleTitle: Streamer initiation in liquid hydrocarbons
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: Electrical breakdown in liquid hydrocarbons is preceeded by the development of streamers [1-3]. Their growth can be studied using optical techniques [4-6]. In earlier studies, the primary interest was in streamer propagation rather than streamer initiation. A factor contributing to this emphasis was the use of low magnification (about 0.5x to 5x) to record events in the entire inter elect rode gap. To study initiation, the present authors earlier [7] acquired data using a magnification of about 30x. That work suggested that even higher magnification was necessary. Here, results are given using 93x magnification and a framing rate of 2×10<sup>7</sup> frames/s under divergent and convergent electric fields. At this level of magnification, it is possible to resolve distances of the order of 10 μπι and, thus, some aspects of the growth of both negative and positive streamers.

articleTitle: Water measurements in XLPE cables
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: The water content in buried high-voltage cables is of great industrial interest, especially in view of the treeing observed in crosslinked polyethylene (XLPE) cables in the presence of water (1–3). It is not yet clear, however, if a minimum water content exists above which tree growth is initiated. Although the saturated-water content of PE is about 10–30 ppm at room temperature, much larger water contents have been measured in treed cables (2, 3). The water absorption and diffusion mechanisms in XLPE are also far less documented than those in PE. Several techniques exist for measuring water in PE or XLPE but none have proven entirely reliable, especially with XLPE and it is therefore of prime importance to determine the parameters that affect the precision and reliability of water measurements in cables.

articleTitle: Aging performance of miniature cable extruded with a commercial tree retardant XLPE insulation
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: Recent field failure data reported in the literature (1, 2, 3) indicate an upward trend in the failure rate of XLPE insulated distribution cables. It is generally agreed that many of these failures which are non-mechanical in nature can be attributed to insulation degradation by water treeing.

articleTitle: Trapped charge measurements in extruded dielectric cables using thermal pulse transient current technique
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: A persistent internal polarization may be producted in semicrystalline polyethylene by continued electrical stressing. The polarization originates from the alignment of impurity dipoles and or an accumulation of space charges in localized states. Distinguishing between these two sources when making measurements of the remnant polarization requires that the basic characteristics of these two polarization sources be recognized.

articleTitle: Electrical breakdown of n-hexane in a test cell with one rotating electrode
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: The electric breakdown of n-hexane was investigated in a test cell with one electrode rotating. Two different electrode geometries were applied: sphere-sphere and sphere-plane. The breakdown voltage was found to decrease with increasing rotary velocity.

articleTitle: Space charge and ionic conduction in transformer oil
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: Questions concerning space charge and electric field distribution are of great importance for the understanding and development of practical insulation systems.

articleTitle: Polarization of dielectric under the influence of electric and cross-magnetic field
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: The behaviour of polarization of dielectric materials has been the topic of considerable study and research for a long time. The results of extensive research work on some aspects of the said polarization have been reported in the past. But all the work which has been produced so far has been carried out under the influence of one kind of field only. In this paper polarization of dielectric materials under the influence of both electric and cross-magnetic field has been presented which has not been reported so far. A mathematical model has been deduced together with various analyses which will give a new insight into the subject.

articleTitle: Design parameters of the optimum HVDC insulator profile
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: The discharge characteristics of dc insulators under contaminated conditions are investigated. The multiple-arc model, previously developed, is generalized to analyze the three dimensional case of practical insulator configurations. An empirical formula is introduced to account for the effectiveness of the insulator creepage length by considering the actual arc path from one underrib to another (tip-to-tip). Based on this approach, the effective leakage lengths of various insulator designs are evaluated. The relation between the flashover performance and the parameters of the insulator profile is also analyzed.

articleTitle: Kerr electro-optic field mapping measurements in highly purified water between coaxial electrodes
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: Highly purified water is being investigated for use as a high voltage dielectric due to its high permittivity, ε≈80ε<inf>ο</inf>, and relatively high resistivity, ρ≈60MΩ-cm at 6°C. Previous Kerr electro-optic field mapping measurements using parallel plate electrodes have shown significant space charge distortion of the electric field in the dielectric. The sign and magnitude of the space charge injected into the dielectric was shown to be a function of the electrode materials and voltage polarity. For example, aluminum always injects negative space charge, while stainless steel generally injects positive charge but under some conditions has injected negative charge [1].

articleTitle: Test method of rapid thermal endurance for insulating materials — A statistic theory of thermogravimetric point slope method (TPS)
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: This paper shows that the reaction mechanisms of functional failure are about the same as thermogravimetry(TG) test in the TPS. From theoretical analysis and test data we have found that there is a statistic linear relationship between the activation energy E of the former and the distribution f of TG curves. Therefore, the E may be derived by TG. Arrhenius relationship of insulation (y=a+bx=a+E/RT) may be solved with the help of the point slope method. The test time of TPS would be shortened by more than 90 % as compared with IEC 216 [1]. Then its accuracy comes near the latter. This method is very useful for the developing new materials.

articleTitle: Characteristics of dielectric failure in REP rate pulse capacitors
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: Repetitively discharged energy storage capacitors are used in a variety of applications where energy density (J/m<sup>3</sup>) and inverse specific weight (J/kg) are parameters as critical as reliability. The energy density of an ideal capacitor is proportional to the square of the average electric field in the dielectric, and directly proportional to the effective dielectric constant. Since the useful lifetime of the capacitor is also a function of the electric field, energy density is, in effect, a function of the required lifetime and reliability for any given dielectric system.

articleTitle: High voltage engineering in space
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: It's a legitimate question to ask “why is high voltage engineering in space a problem?” After all, we have many satellites functioning quite well in orbit as well as several strewn throughout the solar system obviously powered. Most of these devices however were specifically designed for a mission with just enough power provided for the mission and to be able to communicate with the “Goldstone” tracking dish. As we raise the power requirements, we find that the approach to power engineering used in the past is incapable of solving all the problems which are encountered.

articleTitle: The life of XLPE cable insulation containing water trees
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: The most common polymers used as insulation in high voltage power cables, cross-linked polyethylene (XLPE), low density polyethylene (LDPE), and ethylene propylene rubber (EPR), degrade with time when exposed to moisture and electrical stress. Tree-like growths, known as water trees, appear in the insulation which lower the breakdown strength and cause failures in service. Although there have been extensive studies, the exact mechanisms of the degradation have not been clarified and a valid accelerated aging test has yet to be developed. A good review of the subject has recently been made by Shaw and Shaw [1]. One technique to increase the resistance to water treeing is to incorporate a tree retardant additive in the polymer. This paper will describe the results of tests to evaluate the treeing resistance of miniature cables insulated with conventional XLPE (ST-XLPE) and a tree retardant XLPE (TR-XLPE). Both cables were steam-cured. The effects of heating the cables to 90°C or 130°C prior to electrical aging at room temperature were also examined. Also, tests were performed using laboratory-molded slab specimens.

articleTitle: Pulsed surface flashover across solid insulators in vacuum
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: Solid insulators are an inevitable link in high voltage vacuum devices to support and separate the high voltage electrodes. When the high voltage electrodes in vacuum are separated by solid insulators, the breakdown occurs, in general, through the surface of the insulators and subsequently lowers the breakdown strength of the system. This type of surface breakdown, known as surface flashover, has been a limiting factor in high voltage insulator design. The phenomenon of surface flashover has been investigated by many researchers [1-6]. However, the basic mechanism leading to this type of breakdown has not been well understood to date.

articleTitle: Dielectric processes in heavy oils II. effects of plasticizers on the glass transition
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: We showed in a previous report (1) that the dielectric response of heavy residual petroleum streams appears very similar to that of polar polymers. At ambient temperatures, the dispersion in the dielectric permittivity and the appearance of dielectric loss occur in the audio frequency range, the data can be presented as a Cole-Cole plot, and the enthalpy of relaxation can be calculated. This is somewhat unexpected because these fluids contain a complicated mixture of molecules, and there is no obvious repeat dipole unit as in a polymer; an averaging process may be taking place.

articleTitle: Streamer propagation times along insulator surfaces in transformer oil
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: The electrical failure of practical oil insulated apparatus often develops as a surface flashover along the interface of a solid dielectric support and the oil. While there is substantial reported information about breakdown and streamer propagation in plain oil gaps, there is little comparable information about the surface flashover case. The studies reported here concern measured surface flashover characteristics and mechanisms of a point-to-plane gap with a solid dielectric surface perpendicular to the plane bridging the gap. A nanosecond risetime step voltage was applied, and the currents and time to breakdown were determined by an electro-optic coupling method.

articleTitle: An experimental investigation on the degradation mechanism of ZnO varistors
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: By the degradation of the ZnO varistor, we mean its permanent deviation from the original nonlinear V-I characteristics. Experimental results show that this phenomenon can be observed not only in microampere current but also in ampere current. It is well known that the nonlinear V-I characteristics within the range of microcurrent and large current are governed by the principle of Schottky transmission and the tunneling effect respectively. The phenomenon of degradation of this kind of varistor in the range of microcurrent is undoubtedly associated with the deformation of the Schottky barriers in it/1–2/. However, such an association exists only in a definite range of current. Beyond this range(e.g. over scores of mA), the mechanism of degradation of the ZnO varistor will have nothing to do with Schottky barriers. The problem of how it will be governed by certain laws is what will be discussed in this paper.

articleTitle: Life testing and reliability estimation of epoxy cast resin materials
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: The tropical coastline environment has deterious effect on the properties and ageing pattern of dielectric materials. A study has been carried out to establish the correlation factor between humidity and internal discharges characteristics of epoxy resin materials. From the tests conducted and by using IR technique, the ingress of moisture into the cast epoxy resin has been established. A sharp increase in the value of dissipation factor, partial discharge level and decrease in electrical withstand strength have also been observed. These data serve the basis for establishing a new life testing methodology which includes high humid conditioning before testing materials for reliability.

articleTitle: The effect of additives on the time characteristics of a liquid trigatron
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: In the first publication on a trigatron spark gap in a liquid dielectric (1) an account was given that triggered breakdowns occurred at main gap voltages less than half the normal untriggered breakdown voltage. The further publications, e.g. (2), gave information on the time-lag characteristics of both cathode and anode triggered liquid trigatron. From these it is evident that conditions at the anode are of particular significance for the breakdown voltage and also the time-lag characteristics of the liquid trigatron.

articleTitle: The prediction of power factors in cylindrically-shaped epoxy bushings including the effects of moisture over time
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: Condenser bushings made from epoxy materials, such as cast cycloaliphatic epoxy with fillers, absorb moisture. As moisture is absorbed, the power factor increases. Condenser bushings which are employed outdoors are continuously exposed to a humid environment which may affect their performance. A computer model for predicting the diffusion of water vapor into cylindrically-shaped filled epoxy condenser bushings has been developed. The model was used to determine the internal moisture concentrations and the corresponding effect on the power factor in the bushings over a twenty year period. Results and conclusions have been identified.

articleTitle: Force-free flow involvement in charge transport through dielectric fluids under time varying applied stress
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: When dielectric oil is subjected to sufficiently high electric stress, electrons can be injected from the cathode and trapped, whereupon the charged fluid is driven away by the field. Experiments have been carried out into this high stress regime using a repetitive linearly rising and falling voltage ramp resulting in a current flow proportional to a simple power of the value of the applied voltage [1]. As electrons are injected and driven away from the cathode by a distance dx in time dt, the rising stress will promote stronger injection and the trapped electron density will develop an upstream directed gradient. A cathode directed charge gradient implanted thus into the dielectric fluid in an applied electric field is inherently instable with respect to the Rayleigh-Taylor mode. The gradient of electrical energy density ρ<inf>e</inf>V can be expanded to provide −ρ<inf>e</inf><sup>−1</sup>∇(ρ<inf>e</inf>V) = −∇V − V∇ρ<inf>e</inf>/ρ<inf>e</inf> ≡ E', (1) in which the first term is electrostatic while the residual one arises from the implanted gradient which will appear to enhance the field when directed against the potential gradient. Steady growth of the instability will take place when the viscous body force η curl ω resulting from the development of vorticity is balanced by V∇ρ<inf>e</inf> and steady rotation ensues.

articleTitle: Fourier transform infrared spectroscopic study of aging in commercial polyurethane
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: Satellite electronics systems may function for years before failing due to a shorted-out component. If the insulation is considered to be perfectly inert, then such failures would be inexplicable in terms of events intrinsic to the material. However, modern research, as summarized, for example, in Ref. [1], has identified many physical and chemical changes which may occur in the dielectric before breakdown. Hence, a polymer dielectric is not inert and may be more accurately thought of as a seething molecular and electronic cauldron, which gradually drifts in the direction of diminished resistance to applied electrical stress. After a time, which appears indefinite only as long as we have not adequately characterized the system, the constant electrical stress shorts out the degraded insulation.

articleTitle: Bipolar charge transport analysis in high voltage stressed dielectrics
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: Modern pulse power machines commonly use deionized water in intermediate energy storage capacitors. Recent work has shown that charge injection phenomena can play an important role in determining the limits of performance of the dielectric [1]. For unipolar conduction, this anomalous behavior was shown to be due to injected charge that increases the effective ohmic conductivity σ to σ+qμ, where q was the time and space dependent charge density with mobility μ of the single charge carrier.

articleTitle: Uniform field breakdown of binary mixtures
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: The main objective of this work is to develop a way of predicting the breakdown voltage of a gas mixture from the sole knowledge of the behavior of its components. An earlier attempt to achieve this goal proved to be unsatisfactory[1].

articleTitle: Characterization of the glass transition region using automated dielectric measurements
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: The physics of slow relaxation processes in glass forming liquids continues to interest many workers. Substantial progress has been made on the phenomenological understanding of the the thermodynamic recovery process due to Moynihan and co-workers[1, 2, 3] and Kovacs and co-workers[4, 5]. They introduce a distribution of relaxation times superimposed on the nonlinear dependence of relaxation time on the change of the structure. Some questions remain unresolved with respect to the relationship between dielectric relaxation time and the volume or enthalpy relaxation time.

articleTitle: Temperature dependence of the resistivity of dielectric materials
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: The electrical conductivity, σ, can be written in terms of the Kubo-Greenwood equation as a function of energy, E, and the temperature, T, as σ(E, T) = ∫N(E, T) f(E, T) ê μ(E, T) dE, where N(E, T) is the electron density of states function (1). The Fermi function, f(E, T), is given by, f(E, T) = (1 + exp(E − E<inf>f</inf>)/kT)<sup>−1</sup>. (2) Here ê is the electronic charge, and μ(E, T) is the charge carrier mobility. If one makes the assumption that N(E, T) is independent of temperature (2), and likewise for μ(E, T), then the temperature dependence of σ(E, T) should be that given by f(E, T). It is well known that the temperature dependence of the Fermi function does not in genera I describe the temperature dependence of the conductivity of materials.

articleTitle: Charge transport in Kapton
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: Due to its excellent thermal, mechanical, chemical and electrical properties, Kapton is used in demanding microelectronic, aircraft, and space applications. In spite of these uses, the conduction mechanism in this material is presently not well understood. Previous experiments [1-7] were mostly carried out on samples metalized on both surfaces and exposed to a bias. Thus, a clear distinction between bulk-controlled and interface-controlled phenomena was not possible. Interpretations of the experimental data obtained in the temperature range 100 to 300°C and at electric fields of 100 to 500 kV/cm were generally attempted in terms of an ionic hopping mechanism.

articleTitle: Giant orbital materials and their dielectric properties
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: In the course of studying the properties of highly conjugated polymers we found that long range orbital delocalization conferred unexpected properties. The presence of giant electronic orbitals made these materials electroactive yet very stable. A new mode of electronic polarizability, a giant nomadic polarization resulted, [1-3] making these organic polymers among the most polarizable materials ever encountered. In addition, yet other attributes could be found, such as remanent magnetization [4], or metallic conductivity, or unusual pressure sensitivity. The giant orbital concept opens up new vistas of materials properties.

articleTitle: Internal discharge analysis
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: The Combined Release Radiation Effects Satellite (CRRES) will be launched in 1987 to map out the radiation belts surrounding Earth. One of the experiments on the CRRES is the Internal Discharge Monitor (IDM), which will measure the characteristics of discharges caused by charged particles which penetrate samples. These discharges are related to the Lichtenberg patterns caused in plastics, which have been radiated by electrons [1]. The IDM has three objectives: 1) to confirm the existence of internal discharges on operating spacecraft; 2) to validate ground simulations and test techniques by measuring the characteristics of discharges in space; and, 3) to provide data on internal discharges to refine predictive models.

articleTitle: Natural electret behavior of polymers detected by Spontaneous Electrical Current (SEC) measurements
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: When a polymer sample is heated up at a constant heating rate in a capacitor arrangement (Fig. 1), a potential difference (SEP = Spontaneous Electrical Potential) or a SEC (Spontaneous Electrical Current) can be measured with no bias voltage being applied and with no prepolarization of the sample. We investigated several polymers and found this effect in every case. In comparison to TSD — (Thermally Stimulated Discharge) measurements in the most cases we found more and reproducible peaks in the SEC measurements, but at a much lower level. It should be mentioned that the polarity of the current peaks in SEC measurements is not reproducible.

articleTitle: Measurement of surface charges on the barrier and their effect on the oil gap breakdown
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: The breakdown voltage in a point-plane oil gap is affected by the insertion of barriers in the gap. In an air gap, similar effect was already reported in 1930 by Marx [1] and Roser [2], and was recently studied in detail by Okumura [3] and Kouno [4].

articleTitle: Electrical properties of electron-beam evaporated CO-Al2O3 cermet coatings
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: Metal-insulator mixtures, so called cermets, are important for various technological applications as well as from a basic science viewpoint. This paper presents initial results from a study of the electrical properties of Co-Al<inf>2</inf>O<inf>3</inf> composites. We have measured the frequency dependent dielectric function in the range 10<sup>−1</sup>1–10<sup>−7</sup> Hz, and the field dependence of the dc conductivity. The Co-Al<inf>2</inf>O<inf>3</inf> cermet films were prepared by simultaneous evaporation of the constituents from separate electron-beam sources onto metal coated glass slides. Thicknesses and volume fractions of cobalt in the coatings were measured by stylus profilometry [1]. Electron microscopy showed that the films consist of very small cobalt particles, with sizes in the range 10–20Å, dispersed in an amorphous oxide matrix [1]. The matrix is not pure AI2O3; measurements of crystal field splittings showed [2] that the oxide contains up to 7 vol.% cobalt ions. Appreciable particle formation takes place only when the cobalt content is higher than this percentage. We have studied the electrical properties of a number of films with cobalt volume fractions, so called filling factors, below 0.20. This implies that we consider only insulating films with compositions below the percolation threshold [1].

articleTitle: Simulation and verification of transient EHD motion in a stressed oil duct
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: It has been established that dielectric liquids under sustained electric stress are set into electrohydrodynamic (EHD) motion. This results from the interaction between the electric field and space charge in the liquid. The patterns of such motion for parallel electrode geometry [1 5] reveal the existence of EHD instabilities at intermediate voltages. The variations of break down statistical parameters, light and current pulse activity with flow velocity for circulating liquids have also been explored in detail [1,6] and exhibit reproducible patterns. In order to explain the variations of liquid dielectric behavior with flow velocity, the transient EHD motion has been simulated [1] for both stationary and circulating liquids. The results highlight the patterns of liquid motion and explain the EHD instabilities. In addition, they indicate a possible mechanism for the variation of mean breakdown strength and other parameters with flow velocity.

articleTitle: A new finite element technique for the solution of semi-open boundaries
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: A practical finite element scheme is presented for the solution of open boundary problems. The region is considered as an open boundary annexed with a small closed boundary. The open boundary is modelled by the ballooning procedure and the results of the open boundary become the boundary conditions of the inner closed region, which is subsequently modelled by the conventional finite element method, thus enabling larger number of elements to be used for the interior. Good accuracy is therefore realised. The scheme has been applied to a high voltage current transformer and the potential diagrams so obtained for a few test configurations are presented.

articleTitle: The future of high voltage transmission
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: One of the most controversial subjects in recent times in the electric utility industry has been that of transmission. More specifically, the controversy centers around the question of “transmission access.” That is the latest buzz word to describe a proposal that would make utility transmission lines common carriers for anyone wishing to move a block of power. This being a meeting that is concerned primarily with electrical insulation and dielectric phenomenon, I won't dwell on these institutional problems despite the fact that they may have considerable impact on the course of future transmission systems.

articleTitle: Solid breakdown process from the viewpoint of the nature of pre-breakdown current
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: Much study has been done on electrical breakdown of polymeric insulating materials owing to their practical significance [1]. Many unknowns, however, remain about the electrical breakdown mechanism [2,3]. One of the main reasons exists in few understanding on pre-breakdown phenomena directly leading to breakdown from the experimental side, especially such as conduction current just prior to breakdown [4,5].

articleTitle: Characterization of EPR insulators by viscoelastic methods
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: A new type of overhead power line insulators has appeared on the market in recent years. These composite insulators consist of a load bearing FRP rod covered with rubber weathersheds. This paper is concerned with the characterization as well as the evaluation of the long term performance in service of these rubber materials. Degradation of the sheds during service is caused mainly by environmental factors among which the most severe include sunlight, moisture, ice, acid rain and air pollutants. Also, electrical degradation due to high voltage effects (surface discharges, corona, flashover, etc.), although of lesser occurrence, may come into play during loss of performance in service.

articleTitle: Effect of point cathode and point anode on conduction and burst current in an inhomogeneous field for inservice transformer oil
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: This paper presents a study on the effect of point cathode and point anode on conduction and burst currents in transformer oil under high field. It has been found that the current in point cathode is higher than in point anode. Field emission satisfies the Fowler-Nordheim relationship in both cases within a range of applied voltage, and above which space charge contribution becomes dominant. The rate of current decrease in point anode is faster than point cathode. The amplitude of UDI-Burst in point cathode is larger than point anode. The total number of burst per minute is larger for point anode than the point cathode. The condition mechanism is discussed and the role of liquid/metal interface is emphasized.

articleTitle: Integrated measuring system for evaluation of the deterioration of lightly polluted epoxy insulators under humid conditions
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: During the last 10 years, a considerable number of synthetic insulation breakdowns have been registered in outdoor enclosed substations. At the worst, the insulation breaks down already in the course of a few years after the installations have been put into operation. The failures have been found to be caused by a combination of humidity, pollution, and sometimes inadequate designs.

articleTitle: The influence of partial discharges and related phenomena on the operation of oil insulation systems at very high electrical stresses
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: Operation of mineral oil insulation systems at increasingly high electrical stresses is limited by various forms of partial discharge (PD) activity and by positive streamer initiation from highly stressed electrodes. In this paper, the inception stresses and magnitudes of a wide variety of PD common to oil insulation systems are examined, together with the 60 Hz peak and impulse onset voltages for positive streamers and their propagation distance from sharp-edged electrodes. From these data a PD mode, magnitude and inception stress chart was prepared together with a minimum voltage breakdown curve versus distance, which represents a worst case condition which is similar for both 60 Hz peak and impulse voltages. With the PD chart and breakdown curve, an assessment can be made of the operation of oil insulation systems at very high electrical stresses and the high voltage performance of oil compared with that of other dielectrics, such as compressed SF<inf>6</inf> and vapor-mist.

articleTitle: Polarization in dielectric liquids
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: Measurements to verify the validity of drift dominated conduction theory, using stainless-steel, parallel-plate electrodes and purified nitrobenzene as a dielectric material show increased terminal current levels well above the theoritical levels as frequency is decreased, figure(1). These undefined increases in current levels occur about fifteen minutes after an ac voltage, well above the thermal voltage, is applied, figure(2). The delay time may be associated electrode conditioning time and/or changes in conduction particle characteristics. Measurements of terminal current amplitudes and phase angles at low frequencies reveal variations which correspond closely to theoritical values from orientational polarization models of particles with dipole moments.

articleTitle: The qualification of “radiation-hard” dielectrics for capacitor applications
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: Specific polymer dielectric materials have been identified that can be used to minimize the discharge of capacitors upon exposure to ionizing radiation. The testing procedures used to qualify the radiation-induced conductivity in capacitor dielectrics are discussed, and a comparison is made of various “radiation-hard” dielectrics that display low levels of radiation-induced conductivity.

articleTitle: Importance of charging conditions on charge trapping in electrets
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: The charging of a polymer film is the basic process in the formation of an electret, both electrostatic and piezoelectric types. Charging may be performed by many techniques[1] such as by electron beam bombardment, by the liquid contact method, by corona charging, by thermal poling and in an ionization chamber[2] The corona charging technique is similar to the thermal poling method except that only one electrode is required before poling. Differences, however, are likely in the nature of the injected charges due to the different ionic species available for injection.

articleTitle: Dielectric and optical properties of nitrogen-incorporated polyethylene films fabricated by glow discharge techniques
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: It is well known that foreign elements incorporated into a material will change both its structure and composition, which may lead to novel properties. In organic polymers, molecular doping by chemical means to form charge transfer complexes has been extensively studied in the past ten years[1]. To improve the photoelectric properties, a plasma polymerization technique has been developed for the incorporation of foreign elements into polymers[2]. In this paper, we shall report some new results on dielectric and optical properties of nitrogen-incorporated polyethylene films fabricated by two different techniques in order to show that foreign elements can be incorporated into polymer films by plasma techniques and may govern the electric and photoelectric properties of the polymers.

articleTitle: A critical assessment of electrical breakdown in liquid dielectrics
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: The early literature on electrical breakdown in the condensed phase invokes three primary processes to explain the mechanism of breakdown. These are electron emission from the cathode, possibly via a Schottky or Fowler-Nordheim process, interaction of the electrons with the bulk of the dielectric resulting in energy transfer to the latter as proposed by von Hippel, and electron multiplication by some ionization process leading to Townsend type avalanches and eventually to complete breakdown. All these processes had been proposed earlier for gases and crystalline solids. Their application to amorphous condensed matter represented, however, certain problems. For example Lewis<sup>(1)</sup> tried to explain breakdown in saturated hydrocarbons in this manner. He assumed that near breakdown electron emission occurred from the cathode via a Schottky process. The injected electrons drifting in the liquid under the influence of the applied field, were visualized to lose their energy to the solvent molecules thereby exciting vibrational modes of the latter. Collisions of such excited molecules were then able to cause ionization processes to take place. The positive ions so produced were to lead to an instability such as an avalanche and hence to breakdown. Lewis' theory appeared to explain the experimental data he had obtained under uniform field conditions using electrode separations of 10 to 80 μm and dc stresses. It was not clear from this paper how the hydrocarbon molecules would acquire sufficient energy for dissociation since the proposed vibrational processes had associated with them less than 0.5 eV. Also there was great uncertainty of the mean free path an electron could travel in a liquid to gain sufficient energy from the applied field. The use of relatively narrow gaps, the assumption that the applied field was the same as the local field, and the lack of information on the electron injection mechanisms appeared to be responsible for leading Lewis to incorrect conclusions. To overcome some of these difficulties Watson and Sharbough considered the formation of bubbles at the cathode surface. These authors such as asperities, electron emission would occur leading to high current flow. The Joule heating resulting from this current flow could provide the energy necessary to vaporize the liquid in the immediate vicinity of these injection sites in times as short as 1 × 10<sup>−6</sup>s. The authors reasoned that once such a bubble was formed it could grow across the gap and form a spark channel. They attributed these high currents to be due to field-enhanced thermionic emission. They calculate a field enhancement factor of 5 and postulate a metal work function of between 0.25 and 5 eVe The bubble model thus avoided the need for an electron multiplication process. These conclusions were based on highly purified n-hexane as the test liquid, two parallel flat electrodes with rounded edges ranging in separation from 60 to over 600 μm, using rectangular voltage pulses as well dc conditions. The attractive features of this bubble model caused Krasucki<sup>(3)</sup> to investigate the influence of viscosity on this mechanisms. He extended the bubble concept to include initiation of these bubbles by submicroscopic particle impurities in the liquid. The author was able to actually photograph the bubble development in very viscous hexachloro biphenyl under uniform field conditions using parallel plate electrodes separated 100 μm and an applied voltage of 22 kV. The attractive feature of Krasucki IS development was its ability to predict correctly both temperature and pressure effects.

articleTitle: Voltage and frequency dependence of the microscopic displacement of water trees in silicone rubber
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: Understanding of the fundamental causes of water treeing appears to have eluded the dielectrics community for several decades. In part, this may be the result of most of the evidence relevant to the phenomenon coming from statistical studies. Such studies often provide contradictory data, presumably as a result of uncontrolled variables and large random fluctuations. Relatively few “trends”, such as the reduction in time to treeing as a function of applied frequency, are well accepted. The idea behind the present study was to make microscopic measurements of functional relationships relevant to water treeing. To the degree that this endeavor has been successful, these relationships may be useful in testing basic theories of water treeing.

articleTitle: The effects of differently prepared electrodes of samples on the measured values of electric properties of polymeric materials
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: The effects of charge transfer and trapping at the interfaces of metal electrodes and polymeric materials should be considered when the electric properties of polymers are to be studied. The free charges injected into polymers from metal electrodes will be trapped at the interfaces, thus forming a homopolar space — charge layer. We have investigated the electric properties of polyimide (PI), polystyrene(PS) and poly(methyl methacrylates) (PMMA) and found that the samples with different electrodes, such as block, liquid and evaporated, have different space charge layers, which can directly affect the measured values of electric properties of polymers, such as interface charge trapping and resistivity.

articleTitle: Dielectric relaxation and measurements of electron beam evaporated dysprosium fluoride thin films
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: Rare earth compound thin films find innumerable applications in electronic and optical devices due to their refractory nature and chemical stability. Dysprosium fluoride films have been studied with regard to its electroluminescence [1] and electrical, structural and breakdown properties [2]. This paper reports an investigation on the dielectric relaxation and measurements of electron beam evaporated dysprosium fluoride thin films.

articleTitle: The real time and statistical characteristics of waveforms from partial discharges in dielectrics
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: Real time waveforms and their statistical properties help to identify and characterize differences in the partial discharge processes that cause them. A special test cell has been constructed which permits simultaneous observation of both the electromagnetic and the ultrasonic signals generated by partial discharges in dielectrics. A basic cross section of the test cell is shown in Fig. 1. Different inserts can be employed to study the effects of different materials and electrical configurations. Considerable effort was expended in the design of the cell and associated apparatus so as to preserve the waveform shapes as well as feasible. The electromagnetic signals are processed in circuits with bandwidths of tens of megahertz. The ultrasonic transducer and circuits have a bandwidth of tens of kilohertz centered about frequencies of hundreds of kilohertz. Auxilliary digital processing allows the selection of particular types of digital waveforms for statistical studies of such features as time between discharges, discharge energy, and phase relationship to the excitation voltage, for example.

articleTitle: Effects of chlorinated polyethylene on the partial discharge resistance of polyethylene
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: Many kinds of new polymeric materials are now used as insulation for power cable and other electric apparatus. Thus, the requirements for these materials are becoming more severe as the usage of such materials becomes more widespread.

articleTitle: Polarity effects of charging LDPE in a highly divergent field
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: The breakdown of polyethylene insulations at fields substantially lower than their rated values has been an enigma for many years. A popular theory has been that space charges accumulate in the bulk to produce points of high electric field from which the breakdown process is initiated[1]. In extruded high voltage cable insulations there are likely to be metallic inclusions present which would provide highly divergent fields capable of significant injection of charges. In the laboratory, the above situation may be simulated by pressing sharp needles into the surface of a slab of polymer and then applying a suitable potential to the needles, while the other side of the sample, with a plain electrode, is earthed. In the present work we have investigated the charge storage in LDPE with points-plane electrode geometry as a function of potential polarity and charging environment by the thermally stimulated discharge current (TSDC) technique.

articleTitle: Electrical breakdown characteristics in copolymers of ethylene and aromatic monomers
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: A new material, which takes the place of polyethylene, is desired to be developed in order to raise a working voltage and decrease thickness of an insulator. There was a report that the breakdown strength of polyethylene was raised by immersing it into benzene for one year because of resonant energy absorption of the benzene ring [1]. By getting a hint from the report, new materials, copolymers of ethylene and various aromatic monomers, were developed and their electrical properties such as breakdown strength, conductivity and dielectric tanδ have been studied.

articleTitle: Investigation on the processes of oxidation and oxidation inhibition of polyethylene
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: The problem of the oxidation of polyethylene has been investigated and discussed in various papers from the aspect of the chemical reactions involved in this process. The main steps are known and measurements of, say, oxygen uptake in thin samples of an oxidation inhibited polymer yield information on the thermo-oxidative stability of the material. The results obtained are valid subject to the experimental boundary conditions.

articleTitle: Application of statistical methods to the design of solid insulation systems
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: Statistical methods involving the Weibull distribution and regression equations to estimate service life from voltage endurance tests are widely used by insulation system designers. This paper reviews the ways in which these methods are applied to the design of high voltage equipment such as cables and rotating machines. The most popular use of statistical methods is to aid in material selection, primarily through comparative tests. In a few cases, the apparent existence of a threshold electric stress, below which electrical aging will not occur, has been used to set a maximum design stress for cables. The credibility of the above applications depends on simple and objective techniques to estimate various statistical quantities. Unfortunately, not all the required statistical techniques have been developed by statisticians as yet. This will impede the wider application of statistical designs.

publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985

articleTitle: Table of contents
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1985
abstract: The following topics are dealt with: liquid dielectrics; electrical processes in fluids; dielectric properties, high-voltage engineering; solid dielectrics; outdoor insulation; and partial discharge and breakdowns
